newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia's emerging market heyday over - Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: Asia's emerging market heyday over - Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: Asia's heyday as a favoured emerging market is over with Asian companies and stock markets unable to produce satisfying returns, Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia chairman Gary Coull said on Tuesday.
"The critical issue for Asia is just that other parts of the world are more interesting - Latin American, Eastern Europe," he told Reuters in an interview.
"People have slowly come round to the view that Asia is not the only growth story or emerging market story in the world and that really is starting to take its toll," he said.

Credit Lyonnais opened its fourth annual Asia Investors' Forum on Monday amid substantial turbulence in some Asian markets. The forum runs until Thursday and brings together more than 700 institutional investors and over 150 companies in the region.
Coull said investors attending the forum were subdued and sentiment had been hurt badly by downturns in some markets.

Thai stocks have taken a beating over recent weeks amid an attack on the baht currency and a poor economic outlook. Fears that Thailand's economic slowdown could spread to the region has also hurt share prices in the Philippines and Malaysia.
"We think that Thailand, Malaysia and (South) Korea will obviously have a tough time and probably continue to do so," said Coull.
"The Philippines we actually quite like in the short term."
He said said investors were facing "a sort of conundrum" as high economic growth in Asian countries failed to translate into high corporate profitability and strong share price performance.
Companies that were doing well were expensive, said Coull.

"The economies were performing well, companies were making lots of money, there was fantastic share price performance and a regional feel-good factor. The consequence of that was that bad corporate managers made good money and their mistakes were hidden by bull markets in equities and a lot of bad fund managers made a lot of money," he said.
"It is a lot more difficult over the last two to three years to make money in the region. There are other alternatives and it is really starting to show," said Coull.
He said it was very unlikely that global liquidity trends which have favoured Asia over the past four or five years would repeat themselves.

"A lot of investors are pretty frustrated by what they see in Asia whereas investing in Latin America, investing in Eastern Europe there have been some very spectacular returns and high growth and high corporate earnings growth at reasonable prices."
Coull said investors were more likely now to take a bottom-up approach, looking at individual companies, and funds were likely to take big positions in fewer companies.
He said although Hong Kong had benefited from some of the flows out of markets like Thailand that may not last.

"I would say most institutional investors are pretty overweight in Hong Kong as well as China. My guess would be that the absolute dollars coming into Hong Kong from the institutions is probably getting pretty close to reaching the peak."
"It is a kind of hangover period for a great party and people have gone to another party."
